material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Solvent S and extractant X are independent benchmark labels, not real substance identities. Equal indices across the two fields imply no shared identity or property. The catalog provides no material-property estimates.

dossier.identity_policy: Solvent and extractant IDs are independent benchmark-only labels and do not identify real materials. Equal codes across the two fields have no meaning.
dossier.interpretation_policy: Treat the marginal profiles as incomplete prior evidence. They cannot identify the best pair without controlled pairwise experiments and do not reveal the objective score or optimal process settings.

property_scope.solvent: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous extractant reference panel.

dossier.residual_policy: The solvent-extractant interaction table, world-level coefficient transform, phase-volume response, and mixing response are not disclosed. The hidden law is fixed for the entire campaign.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

notes.text:
# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
Target partition is governed by a solvent–extractant pairing-specific distribution tendency rather than anonymous label order. The material dossier suggests S2 and X2/X3 may often favor target transfer, but pair interactions could reverse marginal rankings. Controlled pair comparisons are required.

## H2 [tentative]
At equilibrium, increasing the organic share should increase the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory found in the organic phase, while the underlying concentration distribution ratio for a fixed pairing should be approximately volume-invariant. A phase-fraction relationship of the form organic fraction ≈ D·V_org/(D·V_org+V_aq), subject to losses and simulation details, is a testable starting model.

## H3 [tentative]
Mixing mainly controls approach to equilibrium: weak/short mixing should show lower transfer or poorer closure than sufficiently strong/long mixing, after which a plateau is expected. Because measurement noise and sampling are present, a single numerical difference will not establish an effect.

## Design intent
Use twelve independent batches with pre-separation HPLC in every batch, factorial-style variation of solvent/extractant pairing plus targeted phase-volume and mixing contrasts. Separate and retain a declared phase, then explicitly terminate and final-assay every batch. Predictions above were recorded before physical work.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [supported within screened standard conditions]
Target partition depends strongly on the solvent–extractant pairing, not anonymous label order. At the common 0.04 L solvent / 0.04 L aqueous addition / 0.02 L extractant, 300 s at 600 rpm, pre-separation organic target fractions ranged from about 0.152 for S0–X0 (event runner-operation-0017) to 0.314 for S0–X3 (runner-operation-0047). Other observed pairings were intermediate: S2–X2 about 0.187 (0007), S1–X1 0.208 (0027), S3–X3 0.259 (0037), S1–X2 0.230 (0057), S2–X1 0.239 (0067), and S3–X0 0.285 (0077). Differences at the extremes are much larger than the stated HPLC standard uncertainty (0.015), although each pairing lacks replication. The crossed results oppose treating marginal material rankings as a complete predictor and are consistent with pair interactions. Alternative: unmeasured run-to-run process variation; targeted replication would be needed to quantify it.

## H2 [still tentative; targeted test next]
For a fixed S0–X3 pairing, increasing extractant/organic phase amount should increase phase ratio and organic inventory fraction according to an equilibrium allocation relationship. Planned low and high extractant-volume contrasts will hold total added liquid near 0.10 L while changing the solvent/aqueous additions.

## H3 [still tentative; targeted test next]
For S0–X3 at the standard phase amounts, very weak/short mixing should underperform strong/long mixing; strong mixing should approach a plateau. One weak and one strong condition will be compared, but without replicate precision this will remain provisional.

## Phase-retention interpretation
The aqueous-retained final assay in batch 3 (runner-operation-0030) retained about 0.767 of the initial target inventory in aqueous phase, broadly consistent with the pre-separation HPLC aqueous estimate 0.787 (0027). Organic-retained final assays likewise track the corresponding pre-separation organic fractions within sampling/noise/process differences. Thus separation is destructive phase removal, and retention choice must follow the desired inventory location rather than reading phase ratio as a sampling switch.

notes.text:
# Final source-stage partition hypotheses

## H1 [supported in the tested design space]
Target allocation is pairing-specific. Under the shared standard phase/mixing condition, pre-separation HPLC organic inventory fractions span about 0.152–0.314 across eight tested pairings (events runner-operation-0017 through runner-operation-0077), versus stated per-reading standard uncertainty 0.015. S0–X3 gave 0.314 (0047), while S0–X0 gave 0.152 (0017), showing that changing extractant within one solvent can matter greatly. Crossed pair behavior and incomplete coverage mean no additive solvent-only/extractant-only law is established. Anonymous IDs are independent categories and are not interpreted chemically.

## H2 [supported qualitatively; approximate equilibrium model]
For S0–X3 at common 300 s/600 rpm mixing and nearly constant total added liquid, raising extractant from 0.01 to 0.02 to 0.04 L increased measured phase ratio from about 0.094 to 0.218 to 0.409 and organic target fraction from about 0.183 to 0.314 to 0.560 (events 0087, 0047, 0097). These changes are far larger than HPLC uncertainty. A two-phase allocation model
`F_org ≈ D·r / (D·r + 1-r)`
is directionally supported. Derived apparent D values from the paired organic/aqueous inventory fractions and measured phase ratios are approximately 2.22, 1.64, and 1.80, respectively. Their spread shows the simple constant-D model is only approximate; sampling noise, imperfect equilibration, composition changes caused by replacing solvent/aqueous additions with extractant, and nonclosure are unresolved confounds. The model should be used for bounded interpolation, not extrapolation.

## H3 [supported as a mixing effect, plateau unresolved]
At standard S0–X3 phase amounts, weak mixing (10 s, 100 rpm) gave organic fraction about 0.267 (runner-operation-0107), the original 300 s/600 rpm run gave 0.314 (0047), and 1200 s/1200 rpm gave 0.399 (0117). The monotone span exceeds stated HPLC uncertainty, supporting approach-to-equilibrium/transport control over this range. Duration and speed were changed together, so their individual contributions cannot be identified, and no plateau was demonstrated. A decisive follow-up would vary duration at fixed rpm and replicate the endpoints.

## H4 [supported operationally]
Pre-separation HPLC measures both phases; separation then retains only the requested phase. In the aqueous-retained case, the final assay aqueous inventory (about 0.767, event 0030) tracked the pre-separation aqueous reading (about 0.787, 0027). In organic-retained cases, final organic inventory similarly tracked pre-separation organic estimates within sampling/noise/process deviations (for example 0.542 at 0100 versus 0.560 at 0097). Phase ratio after separation approaches 0 or 1 and is not evidence of repartition. Therefore phase retention should follow the predicted target inventory location.

## Evidence limits and predictive scope
All twelve batches used 0.04 mol reagent and a single extraction/separation. Pairing screens are unreplicated; only S0–X3 received volume and mixing contrasts. The study cannot establish general rankings for all 16 pairs, separate solvent and extractant main effects from interactions, identify real materials, or quantify batch variance. Product-in-phase values are fractions of the fixed initial target inventory, not concentrations; observed organic plus aqueous closure sometimes differs from one and missing values were not treated as zero. Predictions are limited to nearby phase ratios and mixing conditions in this synthetic system.
notes.message: Final source-stage interpretation after all twelve batches

payload.report:
Observations: Twelve batches used 0.04 mol reagent and one extraction. Eight pairings were screened at common additions of 0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous phase and 0.02 L extractant, with 300 s mixing at 600 rpm and 300 s settling. Pre-separation HPLC organic-target fractions varied substantially: S0–X0 was about 0.152 (batch 2, runner-operation-0017), S2–X2 0.187 (batch 1, 0007), S1–X1 0.208 (batch 3, 0027), S1–X2 0.230 (batch 6, 0057), S2–X1 0.239 (batch 7, 0067), S3–X3 0.259 (batch 4, 0037), S3–X0 0.285 (batch 8, 0077), and S0–X3 0.314 (batch 5, 0047). The stated HPLC standard uncertainty for these fractions was 0.015, so the full spread is much larger than measurement noise, although individual pairings were not replicated.

The fixed-pair phase-amount test used S0–X3. With 0.01, 0.02 and 0.04 L extractant, while keeping total added liquid near 0.10 L, measured phase ratios were about 0.094, 0.218 and 0.409; corresponding organic-target fractions were about 0.183, 0.314 and 0.560 (batches 9, 5 and 10; events 0087, 0047 and 0097). Thus greater organic/extractant share caused a large, monotonic increase in target inventory transferred to that phase. Organic plus aqueous estimates were generally near, but not exactly, unity, so these values should be treated as noisy inventory fractions rather than exact closure.

The mixing comparison also used S0–X3 at the standard phase amounts. Organic-target fraction increased from about 0.267 after 10 s at 100 rpm (batch 11, event 0107), through 0.314 after 300 s at 600 rpm (batch 5), to 0.399 after 1200 s at 1200 rpm (batch 12, event 0117). This monotonic span exceeds the stated measurement uncertainty. Duration and speed changed together, however, and the strongest condition did not demonstrate a plateau.

Phase-retention behavior was checked directly. In aqueous-retained batch 3, pre-separation HPLC reported about 0.787 target in aqueous phase (0027), and the final assay after separation reported about 0.767 aqueous and 0.006 organic (0030). In organic-retained batch 10, the corresponding pre-separation and final organic estimates were about 0.560 and 0.542 (0097 and 0100). Final phase ratios near zero or one therefore describe which phase remained after separation, not a new equilibrium.

Inference: Pair identity matters, and the results are not adequately explained by anonymous label order or by a solvent-only ranking. The contrast between S0–X0 and S0–X3, together with the crossed-pair results, supports solvent–extractant interaction effects. Within the tested S0–X3 composition range, a two-phase allocation picture is useful: the target has a pairing-dependent preference for the organic phase, while the amount recovered there also depends strongly on organic phase share. An approximate concentration-distribution interpretation gives apparent ratios near 1.6–2.2 across the three phase-amount conditions, which is broadly consistent with one underlying preference but not precise enough to claim a constant coefficient. Mixing appears to control approach toward the partition state, so short, gentle contact under-transfers relative to longer, stronger contact. For phase retention, the phase predicted to contain the larger target inventory should be retained; separation itself removes the other inventory.

Contribution of supplied information: The dossier supplied only marginal tendencies averaged over an undisclosed partner panel. It suggested that S2 and X2/X3 could be favorable and correctly motivated testing those materials, but it explicitly omitted pair interactions, phase-volume response and mixing response. Experiments were therefore decisive: among the eight tested pairings, S0–X3—not a pair identifiable from the marginal rankings alone—gave the largest organic fraction under the common condition. The dossier remains useful as prior evidence, but it cannot replace pairwise measurements.

Competing explanations and limits: Every screened pairing was measured only once, so some differences may contain batch variation. Only eight of sixteen possible pairs were tested, and only S0–X3 received process contrasts; no universal material ranking is established. Changing extractant volume necessarily changed the solvent/aqueous composition, so the phase-amount series combines geometric phase-volume effects with possible composition effects. The mixing experiment confounded time with rpm, leaving their separate contributions unidentified, and it did not locate equilibrium or a plateau. Apparent distribution-ratio variation could arise from incomplete equilibration, measurement noise, sampling, nonclosure, or genuine composition-dependent partitioning. Impurity signals also increased under the high-extractant condition (about 0.054 pre-separation in batch 10 versus about 0.008 at low extractant), so maximizing target transfer may carry a purity/selectivity tradeoff. These conclusions apply only to this anonymous synthetic system, one reagent loading, one extraction stage and the tested phase and mixing ranges; they do not identify real chemicals or justify extrapolation beyond those conditions.

payload.rationale: I treated the noiseless aqueous and organic inventories as complementary fractions. The estimates combine the S0–X0 and S0–X3 pairing observations with the measured S0–X3 phase-volume series and the observed increase in transfer with stronger or longer mixing. S2 pairings were not directly measured, so Q07, Q08, Q11 and Q12 rely partly on the supplied marginal material tendencies and receive wider intervals. Q01 is clearly aqueous-dominant at its small organic share, while X3 produced much greater organic transfer than X0 with S0, making Q06 the supported choice over Q05. Intervals represent uncertainty in pairing interactions, equilibration and extrapolation, not random HPLC noise.

payload.report:
1. An instance-specific prior was supplied: the material dossier gave marginal solvent and extractant tendencies, although it withheld pair interactions. The least-tested self-developed law is that one approximately constant distribution preference can be combined with phase fraction and a transferable mixing correction. Batches 5, 9 and 10 supported the direction of the phase-volume effect for S0–X3, but their apparent coefficients differed, and changing extractant volume also changed composition. Batches 5, 11 and 12 supported a mixing effect, but time and rpm were confounded. Extending the same mixing response to S0–X0 or unmeasured S2–X0/S2–X3 was conjectural. The marginal dossier itself was not shown false, but batch 5 outperforming the screened S2 combinations showed that it was insufficient for pair prediction.

2. I would run S0–X3 at the batch-5 material amounts, mix for 1200 s at 600 rpm, settle for 300 s, and measure both phase fractions by pre-separation HPLC. This missing factorial corner keeps rpm equal to batch 5 while extending only duration; it can be compared with batch 5 (300 s, 600 rpm; organic fraction about 0.314) and batch 12 (1200 s, 1200 rpm; about 0.399). A result near batch 12 would support duration-controlled approach to equilibrium. A result near batch 5 would imply that rpm, rather than duration, explains the observed increase—or that batch 12 was atypical. An intermediate result would support contributions from both variables. A value outside the earlier range would substantially increase concern about batch variability or failure of the simple transferable mixing law.

3. The raw characterization artifacts were not inspected, and the final assays were used mainly as checks on phase retention rather than systematically paired with every pre-separation HPLC result. Purity, recovery and impurity evidence was also underused; notably, batch 10 combined high organic transfer with a larger impurity signal. Replication evidence was absent, so the stated instrument uncertainties could not quantify process variance.

The least reliable predictions are Q07, Q08, Q11 and Q12 because S2–X0 and S2–X3 were never tested. Q11–Q12 additionally require separating rpm from duration despite the confounding in batches 5, 11 and 12. Q01, Q02, Q09 and Q10 are also weak because S0–X0 had only one measured phase ratio and no direct mixing series. Q03, Q04 and Q06 rely more directly on the S0–X3 volume and mixing evidence.

There is a real tension between the sealed report and predictions: the report limited the approximate distribution model to bounded use and emphasized that mixing effects were not transferable, whereas the predictions used that structure beyond measured pairings and assigned common mixing behavior to them. The widened intervals acknowledged this only partially. The predictions also forced aqueous and organic point fractions to sum to one, while the report noted empirical nonclosure and possible composition or impurity effects. That complement constraint is defensible if nonclosure was solely measurement noise, but it would overstate remaining target if genuine degradation or loss occurred. These are prospective-model limitations, not revisions to the sealed report or predictions.
